title: Compare two JSON objects and report changed paths with Python
goal: Find added, removed and changed JSON object paths without fetching an API or altering either input.
intro: Compare two saved JSON objects without contacting an API or changing either file. Report sorted paths for added, removed and changed values. Objects are compared recursively; arrays are treated as complete values.
requirements: Python 3.12 on Linux; standard library only.
Two UTF-8 regular files containing top-level JSON objects.
At most 1 MiB per file. Final-component symlinks are rejected.
limits: Linux-specific open flags. Rejects final-component symlinks, directories and non-regular files. Intermediate directories may contain symlinks; use trusted paths. This is not a host filesystem sandbox.
Deeply nested inputs or unusually long integer literals may exceed Python runtime limits and are rejected with exit 2.
Integers and finite floats use Python numeric equality, so 1 and 1.0 compare equal. Floating-point parsing follows Python's rounding behavior.
Both documents are parsed in memory. Memory use can exceed their combined file sizes.
This output is a difference summary, not a JSON Patch or a lossless reconstruction.
Arrays are atomic: a changed element reports the array path, not its index.
Added or removed objects report their own path without expanding descendants.
steps: Save the example code as compare_json.py.
Save the original object as before.json and the new object as after.json.
Inspect the added, removed and changed arrays. Validation errors exit with code 2.
checks: Six independent fixtures passed in an offline CPython 3.12.15 Docker container.
Checked identical objects, additions/removals, nested changes, escaped paths, boolean-versus-number arrays and duplicate-key rejection.
The fixture input files remained unchanged.
tested_scope: Six independent CLI fixtures passed in pinned, offline CPython 3.12.15 Docker. Additional Linux regression checks passed as part of the VPS test suite, covering size boundaries, invalid JSON, non-finite values and non-regular files. This does not establish behavior on other operating systems or exhaustive correctness.
